title: The Fourth Column of the Eulerian Triangle: ⟨n,3⟩ = 4ⁿ − (n+1)·3ⁿ + C(n+1,2)·2ⁿ − C(n+1,3)

problemStatement.formal: Prove a division-free closed form for the fourth column of the Eulerian triangle: for all n, 6·⟨n,3⟩ = 6·4ⁿ − 6·(n+1)·3ⁿ + 3·n·(n+1)·2ⁿ − (n−1)·n·(n+1), equivalently ⟨n,3⟩ = 4ⁿ − (n+1)·3ⁿ + C(n+1,2)·2ⁿ − C(n+1,3) (OEIS A000498), the k=3 instance of the inclusion–exclusion formula ⟨n,k⟩ = ∑_{i=0}^{k} (−1)ⁱ·C(n+1,i)·(k+1−i)ⁿ.
problemStatement.plain: A fully machine-checked closed form for the fourth column ⟨n,3⟩ of the Eulerian triangle, extending the parent's columns 0, 1, 2. Stated over ℤ cleared of its /6 to avoid division: 6·⟨n,3⟩ = 6·4ⁿ − 6·(n+1)·3ⁿ + 3·n·(n+1)·2ⁿ − (n−1)·n·(n+1), equivalently ⟨n,3⟩ = 4ⁿ − (n+1)·3ⁿ + C(n+1,2)·2ⁿ − C(n+1,3) (OEIS A000498) — the third nontrivial case of the inclusion–exclusion formula ⟨n,k⟩ = ∑_{i=0}^{k} (−1)ⁱ·C(n+1,i)·(k+1−i)ⁿ. The proof is an induction on n driven by the definitional single-step Eulerian recurrence ⟨n+1,3⟩ = 4·⟨n,3⟩ + (n−2)·⟨n,2⟩, feeding in the parent's eulerian_col_two; the only subtlety is the truncated ℕ subtraction (n−2), which is harmless because ⟨0,2⟩ = ⟨1,2⟩ = 0. Verified against rows ⟨3,3⟩=0, ⟨4,3⟩=1, ⟨5,3⟩=26. 0 axioms, 0 sorries.

proven: eulerian_col_three: the closed form 6·⟨n,3⟩ = 6·4ⁿ − 6·(n+1)·3ⁿ + 3·n·(n+1)·2ⁿ − (n−1)·n·(n+1) for the fourth column of the Eulerian triangle (OEIS A000498), the next case after the parent's columns 0–2 and the third nontrivial instance of the Eulerian inclusion–exclusion formula

The induction is closed by the definitional recurrence ⟨n+1,3⟩ = 4·⟨n,3⟩ + (n−2)·⟨n,2⟩ together with the parent's column-two formula; the truncated ℕ subtraction (n−2) is reconciled with (n−2 : ℤ) by case-splitting n ∈ {0,1,≥2}, where for n ∈ {0,1} the vanishing of ⟨n,2⟩ makes the contribution zero either way

The induction is closed by the definitional recurrence ⟨n+1,3⟩ = 4·⟨n,3⟩ + (n−2)·⟨n,2⟩ together with the parent's column-two formula; the truncated ℕ subtraction (n−2) is reconciled with (n−2 : ℤ) by case-splitting n ∈ {0,1,≥2}, where for n ∈ {0,1} the vanishing of ⟨n,2⟩ makes the contribution zero either way
insights: Pre-clearing the denominator is what makes the proof elementary: stating 6·⟨n,3⟩ (rather than ⟨n,3⟩ = …/6) keeps every quantity an integer, so the inductive step is a single `ring` call over ℤ instead of a fragile rational-arithmetic argument.

The column recurrence ⟨n+1,3⟩ = 4·⟨n,3⟩ + (n−2)·⟨n,2⟩ is true by definitional unfolding (`rfl`) — no separate recurrence lemma is needed, because the gallery's `eulerian` is defined directly by the triangle recurrence and Lean reduces it at the fixed small index k=2.

Truncated ℕ subtraction is the recurring hazard in these column proofs, and the fix is structural: the coefficient (n−k) multiplies ⟨n,k⟩, and exactly on the range where ℕ-subtraction truncates (n < k) the Eulerian value ⟨n,k⟩ is already 0, so the discrepancy multiplies zero and disappears. This mirrors the parent's handling of (n−1) for column 2, one column shallower.

Each column is genuinely a corollary of the one before it: column 3 consumes column 2 (eulerian_col_two) as its only nontrivial input, so the inclusion–exclusion closed forms cascade — a template that mechanically produces column 4, 5, … by the same induction with one more substituted predecessor.

The closed form is an alternating sum of geometric terms (k+1−i)ⁿ weighted by binomial coefficients C(n+1,i); read as inclusion–exclusion, ⟨n,3⟩ subtracts overcounted configurations across 4 'slots', the combinatorial content of the Worpitzky/inclusion–exclusion identity.
